# PDPMVAR Library

This package is a implementation of the PDPM-VAR, lgPDPM-VAR, and rgPDPM-VAR methods developed in Kundu and Lukemire (2024):

Kundu, S., and Lukemire, J. (2024). Flexible Bayesian Product Mixture Models for Vector Autoregressions. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 25(146), 1–52. Journal article

## Table of contents

- [Installation](#installation)
- [PDPMVAR](#pdpmvar)
- [lgPDPM-VAR](#lgpdpm-var)
- [rgPDPM-VAR](#rgpdpm-var)

## Installation

To install this package, use ```install_github``` from the devtools library:

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
devtools::install_github("https://github.com/JoshuaLukemire/PDPMVAR.git")
library(PDPMVAR)
```

To rebuild this document and its figures, install ggplot2 and patchwork in
your R library, then run:

```{r rebuild, eval=FALSE}
devtools::build_readme()
```

## PDPMVAR

PDPMVAR fits a Bayesian vector autoregressive model with separate subject
clusters for the full coefficient matrix and the residual covariance matrix.
The lag-specific extension, lgPDPMVAR, lets coefficient groups differ by lag.
The row-specific extension, rgPDPMVAR, lets them differ by response node.

### Generate toy data

We simulate 25 subjects, each with 25 nodes and 100 time points, using a VAR model with two lags.
We assign subjects to three nearly equal groups for the coefficients and
independently shuffle a second set of group labels for the residual covariances.

Data generation details:

- For each coefficient matrix, choose half the entries uniformly to be nonzero.
  Draw their magnitudes uniformly from 0.1 to 0.5 and give each an independent
  random sign. Rescale both lag blocks together so the largest absolute
  eigenvalue of the companion matrix is 0.75, making the VAR stable.
- For covariance group $g$, draw the free entries of a lower-triangular,
  five-factor loading matrix from a normal distribution with standard deviation $0.5\sqrt{g}$ and mean
  zero. Form $\Sigma_g = L_g L_g^{\mathsf T} + \mathrm{diag}(v_g)$, with
  independent node variances drawn uniformly from $0.7g$ to $1.3g$.
  
For subject $i$,
$y_{it} = A_{c_i}[y_{i,t-1}^{\mathsf T},y_{i,t-2}^{\mathsf T}]^{\mathsf T}
+ \epsilon_{it}$, where $\epsilon_{it} \sim N(0,\Sigma_{s_i})$.
The coefficient and covariance labels, $c_i$ and $s_i$, can differ.

<details>
<summary>Show R code for the simulation</summary>

```{r simulate}
set.seed(20261106)
D <- 25
N <- 25
T <- 100
K <- 2
B <- 5
n_groups <- 3

# Scale all lag matrices together until the companion matrix has spectral radius 0.75.
# A has response nodes in rows and lagged predictors in columns: D x (D * K).
scale_var <- function(A, K, radius = 0.75) {
  D <- nrow(A)
  lower <- 0
  upper <- 1
  for (step in seq_len(60)) {
    middle <- (lower + upper) / 2
    companion <- rbind(middle * A, cbind(diag(D * (K - 1)), matrix(0, D * (K - 1), D)))
    value <- max(Mod(eigen(companion, only.values = TRUE)$values))
    if (value < radius) lower <- middle else upper <- middle
  }
  return(A * (lower + upper) / 2)
}

A <- array(0, c(D, D * K, n_groups))
Sigma <- array(0, c(D, D, n_groups))
for (group in seq_len(n_groups)) {
  coefficient <- matrix(0, D, D * K)
  nonzero <- sample.int(length(coefficient), round(length(coefficient) / 2))
  coefficient[nonzero] <- runif(length(nonzero), 0.1, 0.5) *
    sample(c(-1, 1), length(nonzero), replace = TRUE)
  A[, , group] <- scale_var(coefficient, K)

  loadings <- matrix(rnorm(D * B, sd = 0.5), D, B) * sqrt(group)
  loadings[upper.tri(loadings)] <- 0
  variance <- runif(D, 0.7, 1.3) * group
  Sigma[, , group] <- tcrossprod(loadings) + diag(variance)
}
coefficient_group <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_groups), length.out = N))
covariance_group <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_groups), length.out = N))
X <- vector("list", N)
for (subject in seq_len(N)) {
  series <- matrix(0, D, K + T)
  noise <- t(chol(Sigma[, , covariance_group[subject]])) %*% matrix(rnorm(D * T), D)
  for (time in seq_len(T)) {
    lagged <- as.numeric(series[, K + time - seq_len(K), drop = FALSE])
    series[, K + time] <- A[, , coefficient_group[subject]] %*% lagged + noise[, time]
  }
  X[[subject]] <- series[, K + seq_len(T), drop = FALSE]
}

```

</details>

The coefficient array has dimensions `D x (D * K) x 3`: response nodes,
lagged predictors, and groups. Columns 1–25 contain lag 1 and columns 26–50
contain lag 2. The covariance array is `D x D x 3`.
Each element of `X` is a nodes-by-time matrix (`25 x 100`).

Group memberships:

```{r group-sizes}
table(coefficient_group, covariance_group)
```

#### True coefficient and covariance matrices

The heatmaps show matrix row 1 at the top. Dashed lines separate lag blocks. Colors share a
common scale within each matrix type.

```{r plotting-helpers, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

# Arrange matrix entries for the heatmaps, with one row per cell in each panel.
# x is D x P x G: D response nodes, P columns, and G panels.
matrix_entries <- function(x, panels) {
  entries <- expand.grid(row = seq_len(dim(x)[1]),
                         column = seq_len(dim(x)[2]),
                         panel = factor(panels, levels = panels))
  entries$value <- as.numeric(x)
  return(entries)
}

# Draw the true and estimated matrices with a shared color scale.
plot_matrices <- function(entries,
                          value_label,
                          x_label,
                          lag_size = NULL) {
  limit <- max(abs(entries$value))
  y_label <- if (is.null(lag_size)) "Node" else "Response node"
  plot <- ggplot(entries, aes(column, row, fill = value)) +
    geom_raster() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                         limits = c(-limit, limit)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, seq(5, max(entries$column), by = 5)),
                       expand = expansion()) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = c(1, seq(5, max(entries$row), by = 5)),
                    expand = expansion()) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(x = x_label, y = y_label, fill = value_label) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(), panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.7, "lines"))

  if (!is.null(lag_size)) {
    plot <- plot + geom_vline(xintercept = lag_size + 0.5, linetype = "dashed",
                              linewidth = 0.35)
  }
  return(plot)
}

# Stack the true and estimated entries for the selected subjects into one table.
compare_matrices <- function(truth, estimate, subjects) {
  panels <- paste("Subject", subjects)
  truth_entries    <- matrix_entries(truth[, , subjects, drop = FALSE], panels)
  estimate_entries <- matrix_entries(estimate[, , subjects, drop = FALSE], panels)

  truth_entries$source    <- "True"
  estimate_entries$source <- "Estimated"
  entries                <- rbind(truth_entries, estimate_entries)
  entries$source         <- factor(entries$source, levels = c("True", "Estimated"))
  return(entries)
}
```

```{r truth, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Heatmaps of the three true coefficient matrices and three true covariance matrices."}
groups <- paste("Group", seq_len(n_groups))
A_plot <- plot_matrices(matrix_entries(A, groups), "A", "Lagged predictor", D) +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Coefficients")
Sigma_plot <- plot_matrices(matrix_entries(Sigma, groups), "Sigma", "Node") +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Residual covariances")

patchwork::wrap_plots(A_plot, Sigma_plot, widths = c(1.35, 1))
```

### Fit the model and assess convergence

Fit three chains with different seeds and data-based starts containing 4, 6,
and 8 initial groups **in each partition**. All lags share one coefficient
label per subject.

The example uses the default priors and enables both supported split/merge
moves every ten iterations.

```{r load-package}
library(PDPMVAR)
```

```{r fit, cache=TRUE, cache.path="README_cache/", cache.extra=list(X, K, B)}
chains <- pdpmvar_chains(
  X,
  seeds = c(101, 202, 303),
  initial_clusters = c(4, 6, 8),
  K = K,
  n_factors = B,
  n_burnin = 1500,
  n_mcmc = 1500,
  coefficient_split_merge_every = 10, # split-merge freq for VAR coefs
  split_merge_every = 10 # split-merge freq for covariance
)
```

Each chain runs for 1,500 burn-in and 1,500 retained iterations. Check both continuous quantities and subject groupings.

```{r convergence-tables}
knitr::kable(chains$diagnostics$rhat, digits = 3)

summary_columns <- c("chain", "mean_coefficient_clusters", "mean_covariance_clusters",
                     "coefficient_partition_changes", "covariance_partition_changes",
                     "accepted_coefficient_splits", "accepted_coefficient_merges",
                     "accepted_splits", "accepted_merges")
knitr::kable(chains$diagnostics$chains[, summary_columns], digits = 3)
```

R-hat compares variation within and between chains after splitting chains and
transforming ranks. 
Values above 1.01 suggest that more investigation or sampling is needed.
Partition changes count changes in which subjects share a group, ignoring
simple renaming of cluster labels. In the PDPMVAR table, `accepted_splits`
and `accepted_merges` refer to covariance groups.

```{r traces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Trace plots of group counts and four continuous summaries for the three chains."}
# Convert a trace matrix (iterations x chains) to one row per draw and chain.
plot_trace <- function(draws, title, y_label, burnin = NULL) {
  entries <- expand.grid(iteration = seq_len(nrow(draws)),
                         chain = factor(seq_len(ncol(draws))))
  entries$value <- as.numeric(draws)

  plot <- ggplot(entries, aes(iteration, value, color = chain)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"),
                       guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, linewidth = 0.6))) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Retained iteration", y = y_label, color = "Chain") +
    theme_classic()

  if (!is.null(burnin)) {
    return(plot +
      geom_step(linewidth = 0.45) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = burnin, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
      labs(x = "Iteration (including burn-in)"))
  }
  return(plot + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.7))
}

count_titles <- c("Coefficient groups", "Covariance groups")
count_plots <- lapply(seq_along(count_titles), function(component) {
  counts <- do.call(cbind, lapply(chains$fits, function(fit) fit$cluster_counts[, component]))
  plot_trace(counts, count_titles[component], "Number of groups",
    burnin = chains$fits[[1]]$settings$n_burnin)
})

# Plot the same continuous summaries for all three models. When shrinkage
# has a separate trace for each partition, show one example.
continuous_trace_plots <- function(fits, lambda_partition = NULL, lambda_title = "Lambda") {
  trace_names  <- c("log_likelihood", "mean_node_variance", "coefficient_rms")
  trace_titles <- c("Log likelihood", "Mean node variance", "Coefficient RMS")
  plots <- lapply(seq_along(trace_names), function(index) {
    draws <- do.call(cbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
      fit$parameter_traces[, trace_names[index]]
    }))
    plot_trace(draws, trace_titles[index], "Value")
  })
  lambda_draws <- do.call(cbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
    if (is.null(lambda_partition)) {return(fit$lambda)}
    return(fit$lambda[, lambda_partition])
  }))
  return(c(plots, list(plot_trace(lambda_draws, lambda_title, "Value"))))
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(c(count_plots, continuous_trace_plots(chains$fits)), ncol = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Co-clustering probabilities are the fractions of retained iterations in which
each subject pair belongs to the same group.

```{r partition-diagnostics, results="asis"}
knitr::kable(chains$diagnostics$coclustering_differences, digits = 3)
```

### Compare the estimated groups with the truth

For each retained draw, compare the subject grouping with the true grouping
using the adjusted Rand index (ARI). An ARI of 1 means the two partitions
agree exactly, regardless of the numeric labels. An ARI near 0 indicates
agreement close to what is expected by chance given the group sizes.
The table averages the draw-by-draw ARIs within each chain, separately for
the coefficient and covariance groups.

```{r ari, echo=FALSE}
# Compare one draw of the subject labels with the true partition.
adjusted_rand <- function(labels, truth) {
  counts <- table(labels, truth)
  shared_pairs <- sum(choose(counts, 2))
  fitted_pairs <- sum(choose(rowSums(counts), 2))
  true_pairs   <- sum(choose(colSums(counts), 2))
  expected     <- fitted_pairs * true_pairs / choose(length(truth), 2)
  denominator  <- (fitted_pairs + true_pairs) / 2 - expected

  if (denominator == 0) {return(1)}
  return((shared_pairs - expected) / denominator)
}

ari <- data.frame(
  chain = seq_along(chains$fits),
  mean_A_ARI = vapply(chains$fits, function(fit) {
    mean(apply(fit$coefficient_labels, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = coefficient_group))
  }, numeric(1)),
  mean_Sigma_ARI = vapply(chains$fits, function(fit) {
    mean(apply(fit$covariance_labels, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = covariance_group))
  }, numeric(1))
)
knitr::kable(ari, digits = 3)
```

### Compare estimates with the truth

The following comparisons illustrate estimation. They use subject-specific posterior means, so cluster
numbers need not be matched. We average the three chain means equally; all
chains have the same number of retained draws.

```{r estimates}
A_estimate     <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(chains$fits, function(fit) fit$coefficient_mean)) / 3
Sigma_estimate <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(chains$fits, function(fit) fit$covariance_mean)) / 3
A_true         <- A[, , coefficient_group]
Sigma_true     <- Sigma[, , covariance_group]

# Compare subject-level posterior means for each chain and their average.
estimate_rmse <- function(fits, A_average, Sigma_average) {
  data.frame(
    fit = c(paste("Chain", seq_along(fits)), "Equal-chain average"),
    coefficient_rmse = c(vapply(fits, function(fit) {
      sqrt(mean((fit$coefficient_mean - A_true)^2))
    }, numeric(1)), sqrt(mean((A_average - A_true)^2))),
    covariance_rmse = c(vapply(fits, function(fit) {
      sqrt(mean((fit$covariance_mean - Sigma_true)^2))
    }, numeric(1)), sqrt(mean((Sigma_average - Sigma_true)^2)))
  )
}
knitr::kable(estimate_rmse(chains$fits, A_estimate, Sigma_estimate), digits = 4)
```

RMSE averages squared errors over all matrix entries and all subjects before
taking the square root. Off-diagonal covariance entries appear twice.
For the heatmaps, select one subject from each combination where both true
group labels equal 1, 2, or 3. This selection is for display only.

```{r select-subjects}
subjects <- vapply(seq_len(n_groups), function(group) {
  which(coefficient_group == group & covariance_group == group)[1]
}, numeric(1))
subjects
```

#### Coefficient matrices

Rows are response nodes and columns are predictors ordered by lag. True and
estimated matrices share a color scale. The dashed line separates the two lags.

```{r coefficient-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=7, fig.alt="True and estimated coefficient matrices for three subjects."}
entries <- compare_matrices(A_true, A_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "A", "Lagged predictor", D) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

#### Covariance matrices

Both axes index nodes. The same subjects appear in the same order.

```{r covariance-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=9, fig.alt="True and estimated covariance matrices for the same three subjects."}
entries <- compare_matrices(Sigma_true, Sigma_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "Sigma", "Node") +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

#### Entry-by-entry comparisons

The dashed line marks exact agreement. Coefficient points include all entries
for all subjects. Covariance points include the diagonal and upper triangle
once per subject. Points overlap because subjects share true matrices.

```{r scatterplots, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, fig.alt="True versus estimated coefficients and covariance entries with identity lines."}
# Compare the entries on equal axes so the diagonal marks exact agreement.
plot_agreement <- function(truth, estimate, title, color) {
  entries <- data.frame(truth = as.numeric(truth), estimate = as.numeric(estimate))
  limits  <- range(entries)
  ggplot(entries, aes(truth, estimate)) +
    geom_point(color = color, alpha = 0.18, size = 0.6) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = limits, ylim = limits) +
    labs(x = "True value", y = "Estimated value", title = title) +
    theme_classic()
}

keep <- array(rep(upper.tri(Sigma[, , 1], diag = TRUE), N), c(D, D, N))
A_plot <- plot_agreement(A_true, A_estimate, "Coefficients", "#0072B2")
Sigma_plot <- plot_agreement(Sigma_true[keep], Sigma_estimate[keep],
                             "Covariances", "#D55E00")

patchwork::wrap_plots(A_plot, Sigma_plot)
```

## lgPDPM-VAR

`lgpdpmvar()` lets the subjects form different groups at different lags.
Each label selects a full $D \times D$ coefficient matrix for that lag.
Residual covariance still has its own subject partition. In this simulation,
the **true** coefficient labels happen to agree at both lags. The lag-specific
fit can recover that shared structure while estimating each partition separately.

### Fit the model and assess convergence

Reuse the same `X` and fit two chains from different data-based starts,
with 1,500 burn-in and 1,500 retained iterations per chain. The coefficient and covariance split/merge moves run every ten iterations.
A guided single-subject move runs every twenty iterations at each lag.

```{r lg-fit, cache=TRUE, cache.path="README_cache/", cache.extra=list(X, K, B)}
lag_chains <- lgpdpmvar_chains(
  X,
  seeds = c(101, 202),
  initial_clusters = c(4, 6),
  K = K,
  n_factors = B,
  n_burnin = 1500,
  n_mcmc = 1500,
  coefficient_split_merge_every = 10,
  split_merge_every = 10,
  coefficient_relocation_every = 20 # unique to lgPDPM-VAR, proposes change in single subject, single lag
)
```

`lgpdpmvar_chains()` reports diagnostics separately for each partition.
The dashed line marks the end of burn-in. Group counts can agree even when
the groups contain different subjects, so also check co-clustering agreement.

```{r lg-traces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.7, fig.alt="Group count traces for each coefficient lag and covariance in the two lgPDPMVAR chains."}
partitions <- c(lag_1 = "Lag 1", lag_2 = "Lag 2", covariance = "Covariance")
lag_count_plots <- lapply(names(partitions), function(partition) {
  counts <- do.call(cbind, lapply(lag_chains$fits, function(fit) fit$cluster_counts[, partition]))
  plot_trace(counts, partitions[[partition]], "Number of groups",
    burnin = lag_chains$fits[[1]]$settings$n_burnin)
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(lag_count_plots, ncol = 3, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r lg-continuous-traces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Trace plots of log likelihood, mean node variance, coefficient RMS, and lag 1 shrinkage for both lgPDPMVAR chains."}
patchwork::wrap_plots(continuous_trace_plots(lag_chains$fits, "lag_1", "Lambda, lag 1"),
                      ncol = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r lg-diagnostics}
knitr::kable(lag_chains$diagnostics$rhat, digits = 3)
partition_columns <- c("chain", "partition", "mean_clusters", "partition_changes",
                       "accepted_splits", "accepted_merges")
knitr::kable(lag_chains$diagnostics$chains[, partition_columns], digits = 3)
knitr::kable(lag_chains$diagnostics$coclustering_differences, digits = 3)
```

Both chains recover the three true groups in every retained draw at
each lag and for covariance. The continuous R-hat values are close to 1.
Group-count R-hat is undefined because each count stays at three. The
subject groupings also stay fixed, so these runs show agreement and
recovery on this simulation, with no evidence of movement between
partitions after burn-in.

When true labels are unknown, compare the chains' co-clustering
probabilities and check how often subjects change groups.

### Compare the estimated groups with the truth

Each fitted chain stores one coefficient label matrix per lag in
`coefficient_labels`, with retained iterations in rows and subjects in columns.
Compare each of these matrices with the same true coefficient labels. The
table gives the mean ARI over retained draws for each partition.

```{r lg-ari, echo=FALSE}
lag_accuracy <- lapply(seq_along(lag_chains$fits), function(chain) {
  fit <- lag_chains$fits[[chain]]
  lag_ari <- vapply(fit$coefficient_labels, function(draws) {
    mean(apply(draws, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = coefficient_group))
  }, numeric(1))
  covariance_ari <- mean(apply(fit$covariance_labels, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = covariance_group))
  return(data.frame(chain = chain, lag_1_ARI = lag_ari[1], lag_2_ARI = lag_ari[2],
    covariance_ARI = covariance_ari, row.names = NULL))
})
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lag_accuracy), digits = 3)
```

### Compare lgPDPMVAR estimates with the truth

Average the subject-specific posterior means from the two chains, which have
the same number of retained draws. The heatmaps use the same three subjects
as the PDPMVAR example above. The coefficient columns show lag 1 and lag 2
side by side, with a dashed line between them.

```{r lg-estimates}
lag_A_estimate <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(lag_chains$fits, function(fit) {
  fit$coefficient_mean
})) / length(lag_chains$fits)

lag_Sigma_estimate <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(lag_chains$fits, function(fit) {
  fit$covariance_mean
})) / length(lag_chains$fits)

knitr::kable(estimate_rmse(lag_chains$fits, lag_A_estimate, lag_Sigma_estimate), digits = 4)
```

```{r lg-coefficient-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=7, fig.alt="True and lgPDPMVAR estimated coefficient matrices for three subjects, with the two lags separated by a dashed line."}
entries <- compare_matrices(A_true, lag_A_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "A", "Lagged predictor", D) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

```{r lg-covariance-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=9, fig.alt="True and lgPDPMVAR estimated covariance matrices for the same three subjects."}
entries <- compare_matrices(Sigma_true, lag_Sigma_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "Sigma", "Node") +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

The scatterplots compare entries across all subjects. The covariance panel
uses the diagonal and upper triangle once per subject. The dashed line marks
exact agreement.

```{r lg-scatterplots, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, fig.alt="True versus lgPDPMVAR estimated coefficient and covariance entries with identity lines."}
lag_A_plot <- plot_agreement(A_true, lag_A_estimate, "Coefficients", "#0072B2")
lag_Sigma_plot <- plot_agreement(Sigma_true[keep], lag_Sigma_estimate[keep],
                                 "Covariances", "#D55E00")
patchwork::wrap_plots(lag_A_plot, lag_Sigma_plot)
```

## rgPDPM-VAR

`rgpdpmvar()` gives each response node its own subject partition. Subjects in
the same group for a response share its entire coefficient row across both
lags, a row of length `D * K`. Residual covariance has a separate partition.
We reuse the same toy data, where the true coefficient groups happen to
agree across all response nodes.

### Fit the model and assess convergence

Fit two chains with four and six starting groups, respectively, using
1,500 burn-in and 1,500 retained iterations per chain. Both split/merge moves
are attempted every ten iterations. A guided single-subject move also runs
every ten iterations at each response node.

```{r rg-fit, cache=TRUE, cache.path="README_cache/", cache.extra=list(X, K, B)}
row_chains <- rgpdpmvar_chains(
  X,
  seeds = c(101, 202),
  initial_clusters = c(4, 6),
  K = K,
  n_factors = B,
  n_burnin = 1500,
  n_mcmc = 1500,
  coefficient_split_merge_every = 10,
  split_merge_every = 10,
  coefficient_relocation_every = 10
)
row_fits <- row_chains$fits
```

The traces show group counts for two example response nodes and covariance.
The dashed line marks the end of burn-in. `rgpdpmvar_chains()` calls
`rgpdpmvar_diagnostics()` to compare the fitted chains. You can also call
`rgpdpmvar_diagnostics(row_fits)` if you already have the fits.

```{r rg-traces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.7, fig.alt="Group count traces for two response nodes and covariance in both rgPDPMVAR chains."}
row_partitions <- c(node_1 = "Response node 1", node_13 = "Response node 13", covariance = "Covariance")
row_count_plots <- lapply(names(row_partitions), function(partition) {
  counts <- do.call(cbind, lapply(row_fits, function(fit) fit$cluster_counts[, partition]))
  plot_trace(counts, row_partitions[[partition]], "Number of groups",
    burnin = row_fits[[1]]$settings$n_burnin)
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(row_count_plots, ncol = 3, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r rg-continuous-traces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Trace plots of log likelihood, mean node variance, coefficient RMS, and response node 1 shrinkage for both rgPDPMVAR chains."}
patchwork::wrap_plots(continuous_trace_plots(row_fits, "node_1", "Lambda, response node 1"),
                      ncol = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r rg-diagnostics}
row_diagnostics <- row_chains$diagnostics
continuous <- colnames(row_fits[[1]]$parameter_traces)
knitr::kable(subset(row_diagnostics$rhat, quantity %in% continuous), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

For each response node and for covariance, the co-clustering table compares
how often subject pairs share a group. The chain table also reports how
often each partition changes and how many splits and merges were accepted.

<details>
<summary>Show agreement for all response nodes and covariance</summary>

```{r rg-partition-agreement}
knitr::kable(subset(row_diagnostics$rhat, !quantity %in% continuous), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(row_diagnostics$chains[, partition_columns], digits = 3)
knitr::kable(row_diagnostics$coclustering_differences, digits = 3)
```

</details>

Both chains recover the covariance grouping and the true partitions at
24 of the 25 response nodes in every retained draw. One chain has some
different assignments at node 7. Compared with the same example with
relocation disabled, the largest co-clustering difference falls from
1.000 to 0.047, and the log-likelihood R-hat falls from 1.032 to 1.001.

### Compare the estimated groups with the truth

Each fit stores one matrix of subject labels per response node in
`coefficient_labels`, with retained iterations in rows and subjects in
columns. For each node, we average ARI across retained draws, then summarize
those values across the 25 nodes. Covariance has one ARI per chain.

```{r rg-ari, echo=FALSE}
row_ari_by_node <- vapply(row_fits, function(fit) {
  vapply(fit$coefficient_labels, function(draws) {
    mean(apply(draws, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = coefficient_group))
  }, numeric(1))
}, numeric(D))
covariance_ari <- vapply(row_fits, function(fit) {
  mean(apply(fit$covariance_labels, 1, adjusted_rand, truth = covariance_group))
}, numeric(1))
row_accuracy <- data.frame(
  chain = seq_along(row_fits),
  mean_row_ARI = colMeans(row_ari_by_node),
  median_row_ARI = apply(row_ari_by_node, 2, median),
  min_row_ARI = apply(row_ari_by_node, 2, min),
  covariance_ARI = covariance_ari
)
knitr::kable(row_accuracy, digits = 3)
```

<details>
<summary>Show ARI by response node</summary>

```{r rg-node-ari, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(row_ari_by_node, col.names = paste("Chain", seq_along(row_fits)), digits = 3)
```

</details>

### Compare rgPDPMVAR estimates with the truth

The heatmaps compare the same three subjects as above. We average the two
chains' subject-specific posterior means equally for display and report
estimation error for each chain as well. Averaging alone does not establish
agreement across chains.

```{r rg-estimates}
row_A_estimate <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(row_fits, function(fit) {
  fit$coefficient_mean
})) / length(row_fits)

row_Sigma_estimate <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(row_fits, function(fit) {
  fit$covariance_mean
})) / length(row_fits)

knitr::kable(estimate_rmse(row_fits, row_A_estimate, row_Sigma_estimate), digits = 4)
```

```{r rg-coefficient-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=7, fig.alt="True and rgPDPMVAR estimated coefficient matrices for three subjects, with lag blocks side by side."}
entries <- compare_matrices(A_true, row_A_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "A", "Lagged predictor", D) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

```{r rg-covariance-estimates, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=9, fig.alt="True and rgPDPMVAR estimated covariance matrices for the same three subjects."}
entries <- compare_matrices(Sigma_true, row_Sigma_estimate, subjects)
plot_matrices(entries, "Sigma", "Node") +
  facet_grid(panel ~ source)
```

The scatterplots use all subjects. The covariance panel counts each
diagonal and upper-triangular entry once per subject.

```{r rg-scatterplots, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, fig.alt="True versus rgPDPMVAR estimated coefficient and covariance entries with identity lines."}
row_A_plot <- plot_agreement(A_true, row_A_estimate, "Coefficients", "#0072B2")
row_Sigma_plot <- plot_agreement(Sigma_true[keep], row_Sigma_estimate[keep],
                                 "Covariances", "#D55E00")
patchwork::wrap_plots(row_A_plot, row_Sigma_plot)
```

### Compare with separate and oracle VAR fits

Fit an ordinary least-squares VAR for each subject using
`stats::ar.ols()`. Use the same two lags, subject-specific centering and
zero padding as in the PDPMVAR fits. Each regression has no intercept and
estimates its coefficients and residual covariance using only that subject's
observations. The residual covariance from `ar.ols()` divides by the number
of time points.

```{r individual-var}
individual_series <- lapply(X, function(x) {
  centered <- sweep(x, 1, rowMeans(x), "-")
  rbind(matrix(0, K, D), t(centered))
})
individual_fits <- lapply(individual_series, function(series) {
  stats::ar.ols(series, aic = FALSE, order.max = K, demean = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)
})

# ar.ols stores coefficients by lag, response and predictor. Rearrange
# them as D x (D * K) x N, with lag blocks side by side for each subject.
individual_A <- simplify2array(lapply(individual_fits, function(fit) {
  matrix(aperm(fit$ar, c(2, 3, 1)), nrow = D)
}))
individual_Sigma <- simplify2array(lapply(individual_fits, function(fit) fit$var.pred))
```

The oracle VAR fits use the true subject labels from the simulation.
Both estimate a shared coefficient matrix and residual covariance by
ordinary least squares within each group.

- **Coefficient groups.** Pool subjects with the same true VAR coefficients
  across both lags. Subjects in a coefficient group can have different
  true covariances.
- **Coefficient and covariance combinations.** Pool subjects only when
  both true labels agree. This gives a separate fit for each observed
  combination, including combinations with just one subject.

```{r oracle-var}
# Build the regression rows within each subject before pooling. Each
# matrix has T rows and D * (K + 1) columns, with responses first.
subject_regressions <- lapply(individual_series, stats::embed, dimension = K + 1)

# Fit one VAR per supplied group and return the estimates in subject order.
# Coefficients are D x (D * K) x N and covariances are D x D x N.
fit_oracle_var <- function(groups) {
  members <- split(seq_len(N), groups, drop = TRUE)
  pooled <- lapply(members, function(subjects) {
    regression <- do.call(rbind, subject_regressions[subjects])
    fit <- stats::lm.fit(regression[, -seq_len(D), drop = FALSE],
                        regression[, seq_len(D), drop = FALSE])
    list(A = t(fit$coefficients), Sigma = crossprod(fit$residuals) / nrow(regression))
  })
  by_subject <- unname(pooled[as.character(groups)])
  list(A = simplify2array(lapply(by_subject, `[[`, "A")),
       Sigma = simplify2array(lapply(by_subject, `[[`, "Sigma")))
}

oracle_coefficient <- fit_oracle_var(coefficient_group)
joint_group <- interaction(coefficient_group, covariance_group, drop = TRUE)
oracle_joint <- fit_oracle_var(joint_group)
```

Compare the least-squares fits and the three mixture models' equal-chain
posterior means with the known simulated matrices. RMSE is calculated over
all subjects and matrix entries.

```{r individual-var-rmse}
estimates <- list(
  "Separate VAR"                   = list(A = individual_A, Sigma = individual_Sigma),
  "Oracle VAR, coefficient groups" = oracle_coefficient,
  "Oracle VAR, joint groups"        = oracle_joint,
  "PDPMVAR"                        = list(A = A_estimate, Sigma = Sigma_estimate),
  "lgPDPM-VAR"                     = list(A = lag_A_estimate, Sigma = lag_Sigma_estimate),
  "rgPDPM-VAR"                     = list(A = row_A_estimate, Sigma = row_Sigma_estimate)
)

rmse <- function(estimate, truth) sqrt(mean((estimate - truth)^2))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = names(estimates),
  coefficient_rmse = vapply(estimates, function(fit) rmse(fit$A, A_true), numeric(1)),
  covariance_rmse = vapply(estimates, function(fit) rmse(fit$Sigma, Sigma_true), numeric(1)),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = 4)
```

Pooling by coefficient group gives the more accurate oracle coefficient
estimates. Pooling by both labels gives the more accurate oracle covariance
estimates, but divides subjects who share the same coefficient matrix into
smaller groups. The mixture models can share coefficients and covariances
across different sets of subjects.
